Empirical Research Plan  
Long-run Earnings Effects of Vietnam-Era Military Service (1950–1953 Birth Cohorts)

------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy  
------------------------------------------------------------------
Method: Instrumental-Variables (2SLS) design that exploits the randomized draft-lottery numbers (RSNs) as an instrument for actually serving in the military.  
Rationale:  
• RSNs were assigned in a televised drawing, so conditional on birth-year and race they are as-good-as randomly distributed.  
• Induction risk jumped discontinuously at the annually announced “draft-eligibility ceiling.” Below the ceiling, the probability of serving rose sharply; above it, it fell abruptly. Yet eligibility itself had no direct effect on later civilian earnings except through the increased likelihood of military service.  
• Because many men with low numbers still avoided service (medical deferments, schooling) and some high-number men volunteered, the design is “fuzzy”; 2SLS appropriately scales the reduced-form effect by the first-stage take-up differential.

Event-study plots of reduced-form earnings (by RSN bins) will complement the IV estimates and document dynamic effects before, during, and after potential service.

------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control  
------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment Variable  
Treated = 1 if individual ever served on active duty in the U.S. Armed Forces between 1970 and 1975 (Vietnam-era cohort), 0 otherwise.

Instrument / Eligibility  
Z = 1 if RSN ≤ draft-eligibility ceiling for a man’s cohort-specific lottery year, 0 otherwise.  
Ceilings: 195 (Lottery ’70), 125 (’71), 95 (’72). The 1952–53 cohorts, though never actually drafted, faced well-publicized ceilings and therefore responded in enlistment behavior; we use the announced cut-off as if the draft could have been enforced (“anticipation channel”).

Control Group  
Men of the same birth-year and race with RSN > ceiling (draft-ineligible).  
Because the RSN is randomly assigned, this forms a valid counterfactual group.

Timing  
• Event date = calendar year a man turns 19 (typical induction age).  
• Earnings outcomes: annual civilian earnings measured 5–20 years after potential induction (ages ~24–35).  
• Pre-treatment earnings: age 16–18 (1966–1969) serve as balance tests.

Running Variable (for graphical RDD checks)  
RSN ∈ [1,365]; cut-off = cohort-specific ceiling. 2SLS uses the same Z indicator, but RDD graphs will use local means within ±50 RSNs of the ceiling.

------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Random Assignment of RSN.  
Plausible: lotteries were nationally televised; no evidence of manipulation.

A2. Relevance.  
Eligibility must materially raise the probability of service.  
Plausible: historic induction statistics show 20–25 p.p. jump in military entry at the cut-off. We will report first-stage F-statistics > 10.

A3. Exclusion / No Direct Effect.  
Draft eligibility affects long-run earnings only through military service (no separate channels such as psychological stress of eligibility).  
Plausible but testable: we will test for impacts on contemporaneous schooling and pre-service earnings; any direct effect should appear there.

A4. Monotonicity.  
Nobody serves because he was ineligible but would not have served if eligible (“defiers”).  
Plausible in this context: the draft only increased the incentive to serve.

A5. Stable Unit Treatment Value (SUTVA).  
One man’s eligibility status does not alter another’s earnings (after aggregation).  
Plausible given 1 % CWHS sample and dispersed labor markets, though large-scale general-equilibrium effects are unlikely to bias the LATE.

------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation  
------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Differential Draft Avoidance (college deferments, medical exemptions).  
Fix: 2SLS explicitly corrects for compliance differences; we also control for birth-cohort-by-race fixed effects and test balance on pre-service schooling trends.

T2. Anticipatory Human-Capital Responses (eligible men may postpone college/employment even if they are ultimately never drafted).  
Fix: (i) inspect pre-service earnings by RSN; (ii) include age-specific controls for schooling enrollment (from CPS); (iii) interpret 2SLS as LATE among compliers—note any remaining anticipation effect biases results toward finding lower earnings.

T3. Earnings Censoring at FICA Maximum.  
Fix: adjust cell means with CPS top-coding correction factors already available; verify robustness using W-2 total compensation (uncensored) 1978-84.

------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline (executable)  
------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# Libraries
library(data.table)   # fast I/O
library(fixest)       # high-dimensional 2SLS
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Load data
cwhs  <- fread("cwhs_cell_1964_1984.csv")   # cell-level earnings
vprob <- fread("veteran_probabilities.csv") # SIPP + DMDC
ceil  <- fread("draft_ceiling.csv")         # ceiling by lottery year

# 2. Merge & construct variables
data <- merge(cwhs, vprob,
              by = c("birth_year","race","rsn_group"), all.x = TRUE)
data <- merge(data, ceil, by = "birth_year")

# Instrument: eligibility = 1 if rsn_group midpoint <= ceiling
data[, elig := as.integer(rsn_midpoint <= ceiling)]

# First-stage: share of veterans in cell proxied by SIPP/DMDC
# (v_share already provided or computed)
# Outcome: mean real earnings (CPI-deflated) in cell
# Keep post-service years: age >= 24
data <- data[earn_year - birth_year >= 24]

# 3. 2SLS regression
iv_formula <- feols(real_earnings ~ veteran_share | elig,
                    data = data,
                    weights = ~cell_n,
                    fixef = ~ birth_year + race + earn_year)

summary(iv_formula, cluster = ~birth_year)  # cluster by cohort

# 4. Reduced-form RDD visualization (±50 RSN)
rdd <- data[abs(rsn_midpoint - ceiling) <= 50]
ggplot(rdd, aes(x = rsn_midpoint - ceiling, y = real_earnings))+
  geom_point(alpha=.3)+
  geom_smooth(method="loess", se=FALSE, span=.4)+
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, lty=2)+
  theme_minimal()+
  labs(x="RSN minus cut-off", y="Mean earnings")

# 5. Robustness: narrow bandwidth & alternative control set
iv_narrow <- feols(real_earnings ~ veteran_share | elig,
                   data = rdd,        # ±50 RSN
                   weights = ~cell_n,
                   fixef = ~ birth_year + race + earn_year)
summary(iv_narrow, cluster=~birth_year)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results  
------------------------------------------------------------------
Economic theory suggests two competing channels:  
(1) Human-capital depreciation and delayed labor-market entry cut earnings.  
(2) GI Bill subsidies may raise education and offset those losses.

Prior studies of WWII service show small negative or zero long-term effects. For Vietnam-era conscripts, the conflict was less skill-intensive and public support was weaker; I expect a persistent earnings penalty of roughly 5 %–10 % of annual earnings (≈$2,500–$5,000 in 1984 dollars at the mean). The penalty should be largest 5–10 years after discharge and may narrow somewhat after age 35.

------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV design)  
------------------------------------------------------------------
C1. Random assignment of instrument (RSN) ………………… 1  
C2. Strong first-stage (F-stat > 10) ……………………………… 1  
C3. Exclusion restriction credible ……………………………… 0.5  
C4. Monotonicity (no defiers) …………………………………… 1  
C5. No interference / SUTVA …………………………………… 0.5  

Total = 4 / 5 → “good but not perfect.”
